newsitem.title: UK: Schroders moves to make fees more flexible.
newsitem.headline: Schroders moves to make fees more flexible.

text.p: An experimental move by the investment banking advisers in a 320 million stg property deal on Thursday provided the first signs that a fixed fee structure for underwriting financial deals may become flexible.

Investment bank Schroders, which advised Stakis on its purchase of Lonrho Plc's Metropole hotels and on the accompanying rights issue to raise 222 million stg, proposed changing the way institutions were paid to underwrite the issue.
As a result, investors like life insurers and pension funds guarantee to take up a proportion of the shares.

Schroders put one third of the sub-underwriting out to tender to see if any investment institutions would compete to offer lower rates, breaking with a tradition which dictates fees for the entire underwriting process are fixed.
Late on Thursday afternoon, it announced that it had received tenders for around 78 million shares, or 28 percent of the total issue, at or lower than the standard commission rate.
The move, thought to be the first innovation for decades in the underwriting structure in the London equity market, comes at a time when the system is under scrutiny.

The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) has been considering whether to refer the practice for study by the Monopolies and Mergers, but was waiting to see whether institutions would react to initiatives from several industry associations seeking greater flexibility.

The National Association of Pension Funds wrote to members last month expressing its support for offering a proportion of sub-underwriting by tender, so some of the allocation could be underwritten at a rate other than the fixed 1.25 percent.
The Association of British Insurers (ABI) and the London Investment Banking Association (LIBA) urged a similar approach.

"A proposition has been made by numerous commentators and by the OFT that there is potentially latent demand for sub-underwriting at lower rates," said Schroders capital markets director Richard Wyatt.
"We're testing this proposition as part of an evolutionary process which does limit damage to the existing system," Wyatt said.

When an issue is underwritten, the fee structure is typically about two percent, with 1.25 percent for those who are sub-underwriting the issue, 0.5 percent for the primary underwriter and 0.25 percent for the broker.
Stakis chief executive David Michels conceded it had taken him a while to fully understand Schroders' underwriting deal.
But he told reporters "It's exciting to be part of something that has not happened before -- and might save us a bob or two."

It emerged at the end of the day that Stakis is to pay 4.2 million stg in commission, a saving of 400,000 stg or 8.4 percent from the usual level. Market sources said the rates offered were at around and below 1.0 percent.
"I think this shows that there is not necessarily huge latent demand for sub-underwriting, but it may vary from case to case," Wyatt told Reuters afterwards.
"This is the first part of an evolutionary process. We don't claim that this is the end," he said.
The OFT was understood to view this first step as positive.

It has yet to make a decision on whether to refer the issue of fixed underwriting fees to the MMC, but director general John Bridgeman was believed to be inclined to wait for a few months following the initiatives by the ABI, NAPF and LIBA.
In addition, it has not yet published a report containing the findings of a survey of nearly 100 companies which addressed the issue of fixed underwriting fees.
